title: Miyan Taushe, Blended
author: Afolake Lemboye
desc: The smooth version — pumpkin cooked separately with the peppers and blended, peanuts blended in at the end, and the greens off the heat immediately.
longDesc: This is the other way to make miyan taushe and the difference is textural rather than a matter of ingredients. Here the pumpkin is cooked separately with pepper, tomatoes and onion and then blended smooth, which gives a velvety soup rather than the coarse-mashed one. The peanuts are blended and stirred in near the end for two minutes, the smoked fish gets three, and the chopped greens go in with the heat turned off immediately after. It serves two, and the author is candid that this was her first northern Nigerian recipe after years of blogging.
ingredients: 2 handfuls of chopped green vegetables — green, spinach or efo tete
steps: Boil the beef with onion, seasoning, salt and pepper until soft. Keep the stock.
Cook the pumpkin, pepper, tomatoes and onion separately, then blend them together.
Heat the palm oil and stir-fry some onions.
Add the blended pumpkin mixture and the beef stock, and simmer 5 minutes.
Add the beef and season with the crayfish.
Stir in the blended peanuts and simmer 2 minutes.
Add the smoked fish and simmer 3 minutes.
Add the chopped green vegetables and turn off the heat immediately.
chefTips: Blending gives a velvety soup. If you want texture, mash in the pot instead — that is the other documented method (NGA088) and it is a genuinely different dish.
Cook the pumpkin with the peppers and tomatoes before blending, so everything is softened together and blends smooth.
Peanuts blended and added at the end, two minutes only. Longer and they can catch and taste scorched.
Greens in, heat off, immediately. That is the instruction and it keeps them green.

No pumpkin-to-groundnut ratio can be derived from this recipe — 'half a large pumpkin' and 'a handful of peanuts' are not absolute quantities. For the one documented ratio, 250 g to 150 g, see NGA088.
The seasoning cube carries no quantity on the source page either. One cube for this quantity of beef is the usual reading.
Serves two, which makes this the practical version for a small household.
commonMistakes: Blending the peanuts into the pumpkin mixture rather than adding them separately at the end.
Leaving the greens on the heat.
Cooking the peanut paste for more than two minutes.
Expecting the coarse texture of the mashed version.
Scaling up from 'half a large pumpkin' without weighing anything.
sources: Adapted from 'Miyan Taushe Recipe - Hausa Soup', byline 'afrolems' — no personal byline on the page, so credited to the site. YIELD AS PRINTED: Serves 2.

Quantities exactly as printed: 5 pieces of Beef; 1 Large Bulb of Onion; 2 Scotch Bonnet Peppers; Seasoning Cube; 1/2 large Pumpkin (Peeled and diced); 2 Large Tomatoes; 2 Cooking Spoons of Palm Oil; Small Piece of Smoked Fish; A Handful of Peanuts; 2 Tablespoons Crayfish; A teaspoon of Salt; 2 Handful of Chopped Green Vegetables (Green or Spinach or Efo Tete).

NOTE: 'Seasoning Cube' carries no quantity. And neither '1/2 large Pumpkin' nor 'A Handful of Peanuts' is quantified in any absolute sense, so NO PUMPKIN-TO-GROUNDNUT RATIO CAN BE EXTRACTED from this source. For the one documented ratio see NGA088.

Method as printed: boil the beef with onion, seasoning, salt and pepper until soft; cook the pumpkin, pepper, tomatoes and onion separately, then blend; blend the peanuts; heat the palm oil and stir-fry onions; add the blended pumpkin mixture and beef stock and simmer 5 minutes; add the beef and season with crayfish; stir in the blended peanuts and simmer 2 minutes; add the smoked fish and simmer 3 minutes; add the chopped green vegetables and turn off the heat immediately.

DISAGREEMENT ON METHOD WITH NGA088, not reconciled: this recipe cooks the pumpkin SEPARATELY and BLENDS it; the Nigerian Food TV version cooks it WITH the meat and MASHES it coarsely in the pot. These produce different textures and both are presented as the dish.

AUTHOR'S HEADNOTE, worth recording for what it says about the record generally: she notes this is her FIRST Northern Nigerian recipe despite years of blogging, and apologises to her Northern friends. She calls it her favourite and mentions serving a deconstructed version at a Glenfiddich event. The relative thinness of northern coverage in Nigerian food blogging is a real pattern and she names it herself.
reheating: Low heat with a splash of stock.
healthBenefits: Pumpkin is an exceptional source of beta-carotene.
Peanuts add plant protein, niacin and healthy fats.
Smooth-blended vegetables are easy to digest.
High in protein from beef and smoked fish.
culturalNote: That one of Nigeria's established food bloggers wrote her first northern recipe after years of blogging, and apologised for it, says something true about where the written record is thick and where it is thin. The miyan soups are eaten daily across a vast area and documented in a fraction of the detail that the southern soups are.
